chapterBreakdown.gentle: A company wanted to sell more milkshakes, so it asked the obvious questions about flavor, size, and price. The trouble was that those questions kept attention on the drink instead of on the moment when someone chose it. The opening case changes the frame. A morning commuter is not hiring a shake because it is a milkshake in the abstract. The person is hiring it to make a long drive a little easier, a little fuller, and a little less dull. The commute gives the product a job that many other breakfast choices fail to do cleanly. Later in the day the same product can be hired for a different job, like helping a parent give a child a treat without a messy fight. The lesson is simple. If you study the product category, demand looks blurry. If you study the progress someone wants in a real situation, choice starts to make sense.
chapterBreakdown.direct: The milkshake case starts with a bad question. A company tries to improve the product by asking what customers want changed about the shake itself. That keeps the product at the center and hides the real issue. The useful move is to ask what job the buyer is hiring the shake to do in that moment. For many morning buyers, the job is getting through a boring commute with something filling and easy to manage. The choice starts looking practical once the drive, the hunger, and the awkwardness of alternatives come into view. For another occasion, the same shake can serve a parent trying to buy a simple treat for a child without turning the stop into a mess. One product, different jobs. That is the chapter's pivot. Innovation improves when you study the circumstance and the progress it demands instead of trusting category labels or customer profiles alone.
chapterBreakdown.competitive: The milkshake was never the point. A team kept staring at flavor, thickness, and packaging while the real signal lived in the buying moment. A commuter hires the shake to survive a dull drive with one hand free and hunger held off. The category name tells you what sits in the cup, but it does not tell you why that cup won. That missing why is where most lazy research quietly loses the customer. A parent may hire the same product for a different small social job later in the day. That split is the whole opening lesson. Products do not explain choice by themselves. Situations do. Once you miss the job, you start polishing the object and calling it insight. Once you see the job, the product stops competing only with its own category and starts competing with every other way the customer could make that same progress.

point.gentle: Feature questions can miss the real reason a product gets chosen.
point.direct: Product tweaks do not explain demand if the job is still unclear.
point.competitive: Polishing the object is not the same as reading the choice.

point.gentle: The job comes from the situation, not from the label on the product.
point.direct: Circumstance reveals what the buyer is trying to get done.
point.competitive: The moment carries the logic, not the category.

point.gentle: One product can be hired for more than one job.
point.direct: The same item may solve different problems in different moments.
point.competitive: A single category can hide multiple demand stories.

oneMinuteRecap.gentle: The opening move is to stop asking what people want changed in the product and start asking what progress they are hiring it to deliver in a specific situation.
oneMinuteRecap.direct: Jobs thinking makes the buying moment more important than the product label.
oneMinuteRecap.competitive: Choice gets sharp when you study the job instead of worshipping the category.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
A company wanted to sell more milkshakes, so it began where most companies begin. It asked what should change about the drink. Maybe the flavor needed work. Maybe the size was wrong. Maybe the package could be more convenient. Those questions sound sensible, yet the chapter uses them to expose a deeper mistake. They keep attention on the object after the purchase instead of on the pressure that made the purchase happen.

Jobs Theory changes that unit of analysis. The useful question is not what kind of person buys a milkshake. It is what kind of progress someone is trying to make when the shake gets chosen. The chapter's opening case turns on a commute. A buyer needs something that can be handled easily, lasts through the drive, and takes the edge off hunger without creating a mess. The milkshake starts to make sense once the moment comes into view.

That move also changes what counts as competition. A morning shake is not only competing with other shakes. It is competing with anything else that could carry the same commute job badly or well. The category boundary gets weaker once the job boundary gets clearer. This is why the case matters so much. It shows that demand looks random when the company studies the product and looks causal when it studies the struggling moment.

The chapter gets more useful when it refuses to stop with one answer. The same milkshake can be hired later for a different job, including a parent trying to manage a child's treat without turning the moment into a small battle. That contrast keeps the opening from becoming a slogan. The job is not a mystical hidden truth. It is a situational explanation, and situations can differ.

The practical implication is that innovation fails when teams blend unlike moments into one average customer story. Once different jobs are mashed together, the resulting requests blur into feature chatter. The sharper move is to separate circumstances, ask what progress each one demands, and then judge the offering against that demand instead of against a category stereotype.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
The milkshake case opens by showing how normal customer research can stay stuck at the wrong level. A team wants better performance from the product, so it asks what should change about the shake itself. That produces opinions about sweetness, thickness, size, and packaging. Useful details may come back, but the central causal question stays untouched. Why is this product being chosen in the first place?

Jobs Theory answers by moving from profile to circumstance. The chapter's morning case is not about a milkshake lover as a personality type. It is about a commuter facing a specific problem: a long, dull drive, limited attention, and a need for something filling and manageable. The buyer is hiring the shake to make that situation go better. Once the job is defined that way, the product's value stops being abstract. The thick drink lasts. It can be handled with one hand. It holds hunger off longer than many quick alternatives.

That perspective also redraws the competitive field. In this frame, a milkshake competes with donuts, bananas, bagels, or skipping breakfast, because all of them can be hired to handle the same morning pressure. The category no longer explains behavior by itself. The job does.

The chapter becomes more rigorous when it adds a second job. The same product may be hired later by a parent trying to give a child a simple treat without extra friction. Now the logic is social rather than commute-based. The same object is present, but the progress sought has changed. That is why demographic grouping is too blunt. Similar people can hire the product for different reasons, and very different people can hire it for the same one.

The limit here matters. Jobs Theory does not say every category has one clean universal answer. It says innovation improves when teams stop averaging unlike circumstances into one demand story. The practical gain is clearer diagnosis: study the moment, identify the progress it demands, and only then decide what product or experience deserves to be built around it.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
The opening trap is simple. A team wants more milkshake sales, so it stares harder at the milkshake. Should the flavor move? Should the cup change? Should the size shift? Those questions feel active because they are close to the object. They are also weak because they do not explain why the object got hired in the first place.

The chapter's real move is to drag attention away from the category and toward the pressured moment. In the morning case, the buyer is not expressing identity or taste. The buyer is dealing with a commute that is boring, a little hungry, and awkward for anything messy. The shake works because it can be managed with one hand, stretches across the drive, and occupies the gap better than many obvious breakfast substitutes. The job gives the product its meaning.

Once you see that, competition changes immediately. The shake is not only fighting other shakes. It is fighting every alternative that can get the commuter through the same morning. That is why the case matters. It turns a fuzzy product market into a sharper struggle for progress. A stronger frame also makes losing alternatives more informative because they show which demands were almost met.

The chapter would be weaker if it ended there. It does not. The same shake can be hired later for a different social job, such as a parent buying a treat without inviting a bigger hassle. One object, separate demand stories. That split kills the lazy instinct to hunt for one average customer truth. Average demand is often a statistical blur built from unlike moments.

That is where the chapter stops sounding like marketing language and starts sounding like discipline. If you blend different jobs together, you get feature noise. If you separate the jobs, you get something closer to causality. The advantage is not that you suddenly know everything about the customer. The advantage is that you stop decorating the product and start diagnosing the progress battle that made the purchase happen.

point.direct: Feature-first research misses the causal demand behind the purchase.
point.competitive: You learn very little from polishing the object before reading the moment.

moreDetails.direct: The product-level survey is not useless, but it is secondary. Until the job is clear, attribute feedback is interpretation without a cause.
moreDetails.competitive: Teams mistake motion for diagnosis when they tune features before they know what problem won the purchase.

moreDetails.competitive: Without the commute, the shake looks like a random choice. Inside the commute, it looks like a tight operational fit.

point.competitive: Separate the jobs first or your improvements will chase noise.

moreDetails.direct: This is the operating payoff of the chapter. Diagnosis precedes design. Otherwise the team optimizes for a customer average that never truly exists.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
The opening milkshake case matters because it exposes a subtle but expensive research error. A company can work hard, ask customers many questions, and still fail because the questions begin too late in the decision. Once the buyer has already chosen the product, the conversation drifts toward attributes: flavor, size, texture, packaging. Those details are not imaginary, but they are downstream. The chapter asks what pressure existed before the product won.

That is why the morning commute carries so much weight. The buyer is not expressing a timeless preference for milkshakes. The buyer is trying to make a drive go better. Hunger needs containing, boredom needs occupying, and the answer has to stay manageable inside a car. In that setting the milkshake looks less like a dessert and more like a fitted tool. The category label hides that logic. The circumstance reveals it.

Once the job becomes visible, the whole competitive field changes. The shake is no longer competing only with nearby drinks or breakfast items on the menu board. It is competing with every other way the commuter could make that same morning bearable enough. The chapter's force comes from that reframing. Demand stops looking like taste and starts looking like progress under constraint.

The chapter also gets stronger by refusing a single tidy answer. A later purchase can carry a different job entirely, such as a parent trying to buy a treat without inviting a bigger social struggle. That second job is not a side note. It is the opening chapter's first warning label. If one product can be hired for distinct kinds of progress, then customer research fails whenever it averages unlike situations into one neat segment.

That creates a real boundary condition. Jobs Theory is not a license to romanticize every purchase as a hidden life drama. The practical challenge is discrimination: which circumstance is driving this choice, which alternatives belong to that moment, and which purchases only look similar because the receipt prints the same category name? The framework gets sloppy when teams hear one appealing story and assume it governs everything.

The strategic payoff is sharper than generic customer empathy. Once you identify the circumstance-bound job, you gain a cleaner test for design, messaging, and competition. You can ask whether the product helps that progress better than the real substitutes do. You can also stop confusing broad profile data with an explanation of choice. The chapter's accusation is not that firms ignore customers. It is that they often observe customers only after flattening the moment that gave the purchase its meaning.

That makes the opening chapter more demanding than it first appears. It is not merely saying that customers want different things. It is saying that causality in demand lives in the progress battle of a specific situation, and that one category can hide multiple battles at once. The next move has to clarify what progress really means if product labels and profile labels are both too crude to carry the analysis.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
The milkshake case opens the book by attacking a comfortable assumption. Teams often believe that if they ask enough customers what they want changed, innovation will become less risky. The chapter says the risk remains because those questions often start after the wrong frame has already been accepted. They assume the product category is the natural unit of demand.

The commute case breaks that assumption. A morning buyer is not best understood as a milkshake customer in the abstract. The person is trying to solve a constrained problem: hunger on a drive, one hand free, low mess, enough duration to keep the trip from feeling empty. In that setting the milkshake functions less like a flavor choice and more like an answer shaped to the task. The category becomes descriptive but not explanatory. It names what was bought without naming what the buyer was trying to achieve.

That shift matters because explanation determines competition. If the job is getting through the commute, then the shake competes with any alternative that can carry that same burden well enough. A bagel, a banana, a donut, or nothing at all can sit in the same decision set. The shelf or menu no longer defines the market by itself. The job does. That is why substitutes outside the category matter more than category peers the buyer never seriously considered.

The chapter becomes more rigorous when it introduces a second hiring moment. Later in the day, the same product may be hired for a parent-child scene where the real pressure is managing a small treat without extra friction. That contrast does important work. It proves that a product category can contain multiple causal stories. Demographic segmentation fails here not because demographics never matter, but because they are too blunt to separate unlike moments that look identical in sales data.

The hard edge is a boundary condition on the framework itself. One product can be hired for several jobs, so the discipline is not simply to find a job. It is to distinguish which job governs which circumstance and to resist averaging them together into one false center. Otherwise the framework degrades into a softer version of persona work, just with better language.

The payoff is operational. Once the job is diagnosed, a team can judge features, messages, and substitutes against a real progress standard instead of a category stereotype. That does not remove uncertainty, and the chapter does not support that boast. It does, however, replace blurred feedback with a cleaner causal question. Why was this answer hired now, and against what real alternatives did it win? That shift turns product discussion into a testable argument instead of a pile of post-purchase opinions.

The opening chapter therefore carries an unresolved problem for the rest of the book. If progress, not product type, explains demand, then what exactly counts as progress and how should a team recognize it before feature debates take over again? That is the conceptual bridge the next chapter has to cross.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
The opening mistake looks intelligent right up until it fails. A team wants more milkshake sales, so it asks customers how to improve the milkshake. The questions sound active. Flavor, texture, cup, size. All sensible. All late. By the time those questions arrive, the team has already accepted the weakest assumption in the whole setup: that the product category explains the choice.

The commute case wrecks that assumption. The morning buyer is not primarily revealing taste. The buyer is trying to get through a drive with hunger held down, boredom occupied, and one hand still free. In that moment the shake is not a dessert at all. It is a practical tool that happens to come from the milkshake category. The category names the object. It does not explain the hire. That gap between naming and explaining is where weak innovation work hides.

That is where the chapter stops being cute and starts being dangerous to lazy research. Once the job is visible, the competitive field blows open. The shake is fighting anything that can win the same morning struggle. Donuts, bananas, bagels, skipping food, all of it belongs in the frame if the buyer sees it as a credible substitute. Category logic shrinks the battlefield. Job logic exposes it. The near-miss options matter because they show what almost solved the same problem.

The chapter also refuses the easy illusion that one product must have one true job. The same shake can be hired later for a parent trying to buy a treat without letting the moment become a sticky negotiation. Now the pressure is social, not commuter-based. Same object, separate demand engine. That split is the chapter's first discipline test. If you average those purchases together, the insight dies and feature noise takes over.

Here is the boundary that keeps the framework honest. Jobs thinking gets sloppy the moment a team hears one good story and treats it as universal. The work is not to collect a clever anecdote. The work is to separate circumstances, identify the progress each one demands, and notice which alternatives belong to that specific battle. Anything less turns the framework into prettier language wrapped around the same old blur.

The opening lesson hits harder than generic customer empathy ever can because it gives teams a sharper standard for design and competition. Do not ask what this category usually looks like. Ask why this answer got hired now, what pressure made it win, and what substitutes almost took the job instead. That sequence does not make innovation effortless. It does make the ignorance more visible.

The unresolved challenge remains open at the end of the chapter. If category labels are too crude and customer profiles are too blunt, then progress has to carry the analysis. But progress can still be named lazily. The next move has to define it with enough precision that teams do not drift back into product talk the moment the workshop starts.

examples.title: Elena Stops the Feature Vote and Watches the Product Conversation Change

scenario.gentle: Elena is in a startup conference room with sticky notes covering the whiteboard. The team is ranking feature requests for a campus meal-planning app, but none of the requests explain why students open it during chaotic mornings.
scenario.direct: Elena's team keeps debating which feature to ship next. The votes are loud, but no one has described the moment when students actually reach for the app.
scenario.competitive: The roadmap meeting is full of feature opinions and empty on causality. Elena can keep scoring requests or force the team to study the struggle that triggers the click.

whatToDo.gentle: Pause the vote and ask the team to describe one real situation when the app feels necessary. Make them name the pressure before they name another feature.
whatToDo.direct: Stop ranking requests. Rebuild the discussion around the moment of use, the alternatives, and the progress the app is supposed to help deliver.
whatToDo.competitive: Kill the feature theater. Make the room earn every idea by tying it to a live buying moment.

whyItMatters.gentle: Once the team sees the pressured moment, the product starts competing against real substitutes instead of imaginary customer wishes.
whyItMatters.direct: The move replaces opinion averaging with job diagnosis. That makes the next product choice sharper.
whyItMatters.competitive: If the team cannot name the job, every feature argument is just louder guessing.

examples.title: Priya Learns That the Cafe Line Is Hiding Two Different Purchases

scenario.gentle: Priya is helping run a student store. She tells Ms. Alvarez that everyone buying the bottled smoothies must want healthier flavors. Ms. Alvarez points to the line and asks Priya to watch who buys them at 8:10 a.m. and who buys them after practice.
scenario.direct: Priya assumes one smoothie customer exists. Her advisor asks her to compare the rushed morning buyers with the students lingering after afternoon practice.
scenario.competitive: Priya thinks she has one demand story. The line in front of her is about to prove she has at least two.

whatToDo.gentle: Ask what each group is trying to get done before deciding what to stock. Separate the morning rush from the after-practice treat moment.
whatToDo.direct: Split the observed purchases by situation and identify the progress each group is trying to make.
whatToDo.competitive: Stop treating one receipt category as one job. Force the line to break into real moments.

whyItMatters.gentle: The same product can be hired for convenience in one hour and for reward in another. Mixing them together leads to weak decisions.
whyItMatters.direct: The distinction prevents false averages. Different jobs require different explanations.
whyItMatters.competitive: If you average unlike moments, you build for nobody in particular.

examples.title: Tessa Realizes the Same Snack Is Solving Two Different Family Problems

scenario.gentle: Tessa keeps buying the same granola bars. On weekdays she throws them in the car so her son has something clean to eat on the drive. On weekends she uses them to delay arguments before errands.
scenario.direct: The product is the same, but Tessa notices she buys it for rushed car rides and for calmer errands with her son. The moments are not doing the same work.
scenario.competitive: Tessa thought she was loyal to one snack. She is really hiring it for two different family jobs.

whatToDo.gentle: Write down the two moments separately and ask what each one needs. Do not assume one purchase reason explains the other.
whatToDo.direct: Separate the commute convenience job from the social-peace job before making another buying decision.
whatToDo.competitive: Split the moments or you will keep buying one product for two unrelated battles without noticing the tradeoff.

whyItMatters.gentle: Seeing two jobs changes what counts as a good alternative in each case.
whyItMatters.direct: The same item can stay in the cart while the logic behind the purchase changes sharply.
whyItMatters.competitive: One product can hide two demand engines, and that changes how you judge substitutes.

examples.title: Marcus Runs the Postmortem and Finds That the Team Measured the Wrong Thing

scenario.gentle: Marcus is reviewing a failed launch for a note-taking tool. The team shipped more templates and color options, but adoption stayed flat among the commuters they had hoped to win.
scenario.direct: In the postmortem, Marcus sees that every experiment changed product features while none of them tested the pressured moment when users might need the tool.
scenario.competitive: The launch did not fail from lack of effort. It failed because the team optimized features inside a category story they never proved.

whatToDo.gentle: Rebuild the review around when people would hire the tool and what alternatives already cover that moment.
whatToDo.direct: Treat the postmortem as a job-diagnosis exercise, not another ranking of feature hypotheses.
whatToDo.competitive: Stop grading the polish. Identify the moment the product was supposed to win and why it lost there.

whyItMatters.gentle: The lesson transfers beyond food or retail. When the job is unclear, feature learning stays shallow across domains.
whyItMatters.direct: A bad frame can make a disciplined team collect the wrong evidence over and over.
whyItMatters.competitive: Category blindness scales. It can sink software as easily as it can confuse a shake.

examples.title: Malik Predicts One Winning Product and the Register Reveals Two Different Jobs

scenario.gentle: Malik predicts that students buy the store's cold brew because they all want more caffeine. After one week of watching purchases, he notices one crowd buys before an 8 a.m. class and another buys slowly while chatting after club meetings.
scenario.direct: Malik starts with one explanation for cold-brew demand. Observation shows two separate buying moments instead.
scenario.competitive: Malik wanted one clean answer. The register gives him two, and the lazy move is to mash them back together.

whatToDo.gentle: Treat the two moments as different jobs and study the progress each one is serving before making a stocking decision.
whatToDo.direct: Separate the rushed caffeine job from the lingering social job instead of averaging them.
whatToDo.competitive: Do not rescue the neat story. Split the demand and make each moment earn its own explanation.

whyItMatters.gentle: The common trap is thinking one product must have one reason behind every sale.
whyItMatters.direct: The reveal keeps the analysis honest by showing how easy false unity can be.
whyItMatters.competitive: Most bad demand stories come from forcing one explanation across unlike moments.

examples.title: Devon Changes What He Packs for the Drive Once He Notices the Real Job

scenario.gentle: Before, Devon kept grabbing pastries that made the car messy and left him hungry too soon. After paying attention to the drive itself, he starts choosing options that last longer and stay manageable in one hand.
scenario.direct: Devon used to buy whatever looked quick at the counter. Once he names the commute job clearly, his choices change because the real standard changes.
scenario.competitive: Devon stopped buying by category and started buying by battle. The drive got easier because the job finally led the choice.

whatToDo.gentle: Name the situation first, then compare alternatives against the progress the moment actually demands.
whatToDo.direct: Let the job reset what good looks like before you pick the product.
whatToDo.competitive: Choose against the struggle, not against the shelf label.

whyItMatters.gentle: The same person can make a better choice once the moment becomes visible.
whyItMatters.direct: A clearer job changes both the substitute set and the evaluation standard.
whyItMatters.competitive: Once the job is explicit, bad defaults lose their cover.

questions.prompt: What mistake did the first milkshake research make?
choices: It focused on the product before understanding the job
It ignored the price completely
It studied too many stores at once

explanation.gentle: The opening problem is not lack of effort. The team begins with feature questions before the buying moment is understood.
explanation.direct: The product is treated as the center of demand too early. That hides the causal job.
explanation.competitive: They tuned the object before reading the hire.

questions.prompt: Why does the morning commute matter so much in the opening case?
choices: It proves commuters prefer cold drinks in every season
It reveals the pressured situation the product is helping with
It shows that drivers do not care about taste at all

explanation.gentle: The commute gives the purchase a purpose. Hunger, boredom, and one-handed use make the product choice easier to explain.
explanation.direct: The moment supplies the constraints that make the job visible.
explanation.competitive: Without the drive, the choice looks fuzzy. Inside it, the fit sharpens.

questions.prompt: A team knows who buys its product but still cannot explain why sales stay unpredictable. What is the chapter's best diagnosis?
choices: The team has profile data but not a clear job tied to a real circumstance
The team needs a larger customer persona spreadsheet
The team should copy the market leader's features immediately

explanation.gentle: Knowing who bought is not the same as knowing what progress the buyer was trying to make.
explanation.direct: Profiles can describe the customer while leaving the causal demand untouched.
explanation.competitive: You can know the buyer and still miss the battle that triggered the purchase.

questions.prompt: Elena's product team is arguing over new feature requests. Which move fits the chapter best?
choices: Add the top three requested features before doing more research
Ask the team to name the exact moment when the product feels necessary and what alternatives exist there
Segment users by age and income before looking at behavior

explanation.gentle: The chapter pushes the team back toward the pressured moment and the job it contains.
explanation.direct: Choice B rebuilds the discussion around circumstance and progress instead of feature voting.
explanation.competitive: That move forces causality into a room that was drifting on opinions.

questions.prompt: Why is category-based competition too narrow in the milkshake case?
choices: Because the product really competes only with premium brands
Because the buyer is also considering any substitute that can solve the same morning problem
Because categories matter only in luxury markets

explanation.gentle: The product competes with whatever else could get the commute job done well enough.
explanation.direct: The job widens the field beyond category peers to the buyer's real alternative set.
explanation.competitive: Once the struggle is clear, the shelf stops containing the market.

questions.prompt: A parent buys the same snack at a different time of day for a calmer family moment. What does that add to the chapter's logic?
choices: It shows the product can serve a second job in a different situation
It proves the morning commute explanation was wrong
It means feature questions were actually enough all along

explanation.gentle: The second moment does not cancel the first. It shows that one product can be hired for more than one kind of progress.
explanation.direct: This is a boundary condition on the framework. Similar purchases may hide different causal stories.
explanation.competitive: Same item, different battle. That is the discipline test.

questions.prompt: Priya is studying smoothie sales in a student store. What would most likely create a false answer?
choices: Watching morning and afternoon purchases as separate situations
Assuming all smoothie buyers want the same thing because they bought the same product
Comparing the product with what students buy instead on rushed days

explanation.gentle: The chapter warns against blending unlike moments into one average demand story.
explanation.direct: Choice B collapses distinct jobs into one explanation just because the receipt prints the same item.
explanation.competitive: That is how a neat answer turns into a bad one.

questions.prompt: Devon notices that messy pastries fail his commute even though he likes them. What changed in his thinking?
choices: He stopped caring about flavor
He started choosing against the job's constraints rather than the category label alone
He decided all breakfast products are basically interchangeable

explanation.gentle: The choice improves once the drive, the hunger, and the one-handed constraint become the real standard.
explanation.direct: He is now evaluating alternatives against the job instead of against a generic breakfast category.
explanation.competitive: The battle got named, so the bad default lost.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter's strongest warning about finding one good customer story?
choices: A good story should be treated as the universal answer immediately
A strong anecdote still has to be tested against whether different situations are being blended together
Any story from observation is less useful than a survey average

explanation.gentle: One helpful story can still mislead if it gets stretched over moments that are actually different.
explanation.direct: The framework requires discrimination. A job story becomes weak when it is universalized too early.
explanation.competitive: Anecdote turns into error the moment you crown it as the whole market.

questions.prompt: If category labels are too blunt to explain demand, what does the chapter point toward next?
choices: A sharper definition of the progress the customer is trying to make
A return to feature ranking once the team has enough opinions
A narrower focus on buyer personality types

explanation.gentle: The chapter ends by pushing beyond product labels toward a clearer account of progress.
explanation.direct: This is the bridge forward. Once the job is visible, progress itself has to be defined more precisely.
explanation.competitive: If category talk is blunt, the next tool has to name the progress battle cleanly.

coreSkill.gentle: The core skill is noticing the moment that makes a product useful before you start talking about how to improve the product itself.
coreSkill.direct: This chapter teaches job diagnosis: define the circumstance and the progress it demands before optimizing features.
coreSkill.competitive: The skill is reading the hire before you start polishing the object.

plan.gentle: If a product discussion jumps straight to features, then pause and ask what real moment the product is being hired to improve.
plan.direct: If the team starts ranking requests too early, then pull the conversation back to the circumstance and the substitutes in that situation.
plan.competitive: If the room worships features, force it to name the job first.

plan.gentle: If a student business sees one product selling for different reasons, then separate the buying moments before you change the offer.
plan.direct: If one school-store item seems to serve mixed patterns, then split the observations by situation and compare the jobs.
plan.competitive: If one SKU looks like one answer, test whether the line is hiding two jobs.

plan.gentle: If you keep buying the same thing in different parts of the week, then ask whether those moments are actually asking the product to do the same job.
plan.direct: If one repeated purchase feels inconsistently useful, then define the separate situations before deciding whether the product is still the right answer.
plan.competitive: If one habit serves two battles badly, split the jobs before you buy again.

twentyFourHourChallenge.gentle: In the next day, watch one purchase you make and write down the exact situation that made it feel necessary.
twentyFourHourChallenge.direct: Within 24 hours, identify one buying moment and list the alternatives that were really competing there.
twentyFourHourChallenge.competitive: Before tomorrow ends, catch one purchase in the act and name the battle it won.

weeklyPractice.gentle: Once this week, separate one product you use into two distinct situations and notice whether it is doing the same job in both.
weeklyPractice.direct: Run one weekly job audit on a repeated purchase by comparing two moments that look similar on the surface.
weeklyPractice.competitive: This week, break one buying habit into separate fights and see whether one product deserves both wins.

front.gentle: What was wrong with the first milkshake questions?
front.direct: What did the team center too early?
front.competitive: What did the research worship instead of the hire?

back.gentle: They centered product features before the job.
back.direct: The product itself, not the buying moment.

front.direct: Which part of the case makes the job visible?

back.direct: The commute situation and its constraints.

front.gentle: Why can a product's competitors extend beyond its category?
front.direct: What widens the competitive set here?
front.competitive: Why does the battlefield get larger?

back.gentle: Because any substitute solving the same job can compete.
back.direct: The visible job redraws the alternative set.
back.competitive: The job, not the shelf, defines the rivals.

front.gentle: What does the second milkshake job warn against?
front.direct: What mistake does the parent-child moment help prevent?
front.competitive: What kills the insight if you ignore the second hire?

back.gentle: Blending unlike situations into one demand story.

front.gentle: Finish the move: study the moment, then...
front.competitive: What has to happen before you polish the product?

keyTakeawayCard.gentle: The opening lesson is that customer choice becomes clearer when you study the progress someone wants in a specific moment instead of asking only how to improve the product. The milkshake works because the situation gives it a job.
keyTakeawayCard.direct: Innovation gets sharper when work shifts from product attributes to circumstance-bound progress. Once the job is visible, competition, research, and design all become easier to diagnose.
keyTakeawayCard.competitive: The category does not explain the hire. The pressured moment does. If you miss the job, you decorate the product and call it learning.
